title: Rice’s theorem: undecidable properties of programs

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 65–72 (§3.3, many-one reductions and Rice’s theorem; version 2007-01-09)

summary: Use one waiting construction to show that every nontrivial property of the partial function computed by a program is undecidable.
abstract: Could a program inspect another program and always decide whether it stops on every input, or whether it ever returns a particular number? These questions concern what the program computes, rather than how its instructions are written. Rice’s theorem gives a common explanation for their difficulty: every property of computed partial functions that holds for some programs and fails for others is undecidable. The proof transforms a halting question into a program that waits before carrying out a fixed computation. This construction also explains why finite checks on program text escape the theorem, why divergence must count as part of a program’s behavior, and why undecidability alone does not rule out recognizing positive answers.
